Are you a Machine Learning Engineer / AI researcher that want to better understand how’s AI used in the context of Drug Discovery but lack the basic biology knowledge to really get sense of anything you read about it? This blog post is my attempt to provide (mostly myself) the necessary tool to do just that.
I arbitrarily decided to revise the prospective paper “Rethinking drug design in the artificial intelligence era” from Petra Schneider et al. :
Introduction - The Core Problem
The Challenge: Drug discovery is extremely expensive and slow, with very high failure rates in clinical trials. The industry needs better ways to design drug candidates faster and cheaper.
Current Approach: High-throughput screening (HTS) - testing millions of compounds against biological targets
- Hit rates are terrible: 0-0.01% (finding a needle in a haystack)
- Creates massive, complex datasets that are hard for humans to analyze
- Medicinal chemists face multi-objective optimization problems with way too many variables to explore systematically
AI’s Promise:
- Help navigate these vast datasets intelligently
- Augment human decision-making rather than replace it
- Ultimate goal: Generate new drug candidates from scratch (“de novo design”) without expensive screening
The 5 Grand Challenges
Generating appropriate datasets
Generating new hypotheses
Multi-objective optimization
Reducing cycle times
Changing research culture
Generating appropriate datasets
Unlike image recognition or NLP where labels are straightforward, drug discovery involves messy, context-dependent labels where “toxic” or “active” depends heavily on experimental conditions, dosage, and species. This creates a fundamental garbage-in-garbage-out problem that’s much more severe than typical ML applications.
The surrogate endpoints problem is particularly challenging because models are often trained on proxy measurements like cell culture toxicity when the real target is human toxicity. This is analogous to training a self-driving car model on video game footage instead of real road data. Additionally, missing data in drug discovery is not random since expensive experiments like animal testing are only performed on promising compounds, creating systematic bias that standard missing data techniques cannot address.
Drug discovery datasets suffer from extreme class imbalance with datasets dominated by inactive compounds and very few positive examples to learn from. The data scale problem is equally severe as successful AI typically requires millions of training examples, but drug discovery datasets are tiny compared to ImageNet and there’s no easy way to generate more labeled data since experiments are expensive and time-consuming.
Modern drug discovery generates complex, high-dimensional outputs beyond simple binding strength numbers, including dose-response curves, time-series data, and medical images that require better representations and dimensionality reduction techniques. The annotation process creates additional bottlenecks since biological data needs expert annotation that is tedious and often skipped, while rapidly changing biological terminology lacks standardization, making it difficult to link related concepts across datasets.
Error detection becomes critical because even one or two mislabeled data points can significantly skew model performance, requiring fraud-detection-like approaches to identify outliers. The industry faces a fundamental data sharing problem where the best datasets remain proprietary to pharmaceutical companies who guard them as competitive advantages, while public datasets like ChEMBL and PubChem are smaller and lower quality. Potential solutions include federated learning approaches, sharing only chemical transformations rather than full structures, and cryptographic methods to share model parameters without revealing proprietary information.
Generating New Hypotheses
The fundamental challenge in drug discovery is that the chemical space is astronomically large while current screening methods sample only a tiny fraction of it. Even the largest high-throughput screening libraries test only 10^6 to 10^7 compounds, and newer DNA-encoded libraries can test up to 10^10 compounds, but this still represents a minuscule sample of the estimated 10^18 to 10^200 possible druglike molecules. To put this in perspective, the entire purchasable chemical space contains approximately 125 million compounds as of 2015, which is still growing but remains dwarfed by the theoretical possibilities.
This enormous search space makes exhaustive enumeration impossible, reducing drug design to the fundamental question of “what to make next.” Traditional medicinal chemists rely on experience, heuristic guidelines, and loosely defined “chemical intuition” to navigate this space, but given the complexity of human disease, more systematic approaches for hypothesis generation are needed.
Modern generative AI offers a revolutionary approach to this problem by providing a statistical framework for decision making rather than relying on explicit chemical rules. Unlike earlier computer-based design methods that used explicit chemical transformations and assembly rules based on textbook chemistry, generative models represent chemical knowledge implicitly through statistical probabilities learned from training data. This creates a new language for chemical design that’s learned from data rather than hard-coded from chemical knowledge.
These generative approaches offer several key advantages over previous methods. They provide rapid execution speed where new chemical entities can be generated on-demand for interactive modeling, allow quick retraining or fine-tuning for specific projects, offer scalability by accessing virtually infinite chemical space without explicit compound library enumeration, have readily available software implementations, and most importantly, tend to produce synthetically accessible designs, which was a major limitation of earlier approaches.
The field faces increasing complexity as both data and target hypotheses become more sophisticated, compounded by fundamental gaps in our understanding of human biology. This requires AI systems to be highly adaptable since biological assays and knowledge rapidly evolve throughout a drug discovery project’s lifetime. Mechanistic models complement AI approaches by capturing behaviors at different levels of biological organization and providing explanations for how these behaviors interact. This creates a powerful synergy where mechanistic models generate new hypotheses while machine learning models provide data to test these hypotheses, forming a complete learning system through this virtual cycle of hypothesis generation and testing.
Multi-objective Optimization
Drug design is fundamentally a multi-objective optimization problem where you need to balance several conflicting properties simultaneously. A molecule might be very effective at binding to the disease target but also toxic, or it might be safe but get cleared from the body too quickly to be useful. This creates the classic machine learning challenge of optimizing multiple objectives that work against each other.
The standard approach is to find a Pareto frontier of solutions where each solution represents a different trade-off between properties, and no solution can be improved in one dimension without getting worse in another. However, drug discovery adds a crucial complication: we rarely know upfront how to weight these different objectives. The relative importance of safety versus efficacy often only becomes clear through iterative experimentation, making this an optimization problem with unknown preferences that must be solved through human-AI collaboration.
The technical implementation requires predictive models for each property of interest, essentially creating a regression or classification problem for each objective (toxicity, binding strength, clearance rate, etc.). The challenge then becomes inverse QSAR - using these trained models to back-engineer optimal molecular structures, similar to adversarial example generation but for drug design rather than fooling classifiers.
Current neural network approaches face several critical limitations in this domain. First, the data scarcity problem is severe since drug discovery datasets are tiny compared to ImageNet-scale training sets, and generating new labeled examples requires expensive biological experiments. Second, deep networks exhibit problematic behaviors that are especially dangerous in optimization settings: they’re overconfident in their predictions, vulnerable to adversarial examples, and poor at extrapolation beyond their training distribution. During optimization, models will inevitably be pushed into regions they’ve never seen before, potentially leading the entire drug design process astray while appearing confident about their predictions.
The field is moving away from genetic algorithms toward more sophisticated approaches like Estimation of Distribution Algorithms that use generative models instead of crude mutation operations. Modern implementations leverage variational autoencoders and other deep generative models to sample from molecular space, creating rich probabilistic representations that can be tuned to focus on desired properties. This connects multi-objective optimization directly to the generative modeling advances in Challenge 2, since the same models that generate novel drug candidates also serve as the sampling mechanism for exploring trade-offs between different molecular properties.
The molecular representation problem adds another layer of complexity, as standard neural architectures designed for images don’t translate well to chemical structures. Graph neural networks show promise for capturing molecular topology, but encoding chemical properties in a way that enables effective optimization remains an open research problem. The goal is creating representations that capture both structural and functional aspects of molecules in a format amenable to gradient-based optimization and generative modeling.
Reducing Cycle Times
Drug discovery follows an iterative process called the design-make-test-analyze (DMTA) cycle, which is essentially a hypothesis-testing loop. Scientists design molecules based on current data, synthesize them, test their properties, analyze the results, and use those insights to design the next batch of molecules. The fundamental problem is that each cycle takes 4-8 weeks to complete, and you need many cycles to develop a successful drug candidate.
The bottleneck isn’t the computational parts - designing molecules and analyzing data can be fast. The real constraint is the “make” phase, where synthesizing novel molecules takes weeks of lab work. This creates a throughput problem similar to having a fast GPU training loop but being limited by slow data loading. Even worse, teams often run multiple parallel cycles and start the next synthesis round before getting all the test results back, essentially running the optimization with stale gradients and incomplete information.
The data processing challenge compounds this timing issue. Modern drug discovery generates massive, high-dimensional datasets that exceed human cognitive capacity to fully process. Scientists resort to simple heuristics and rules of thumb rather than extracting all available insights from their data, similar to how practitioners might use basic statistical tests instead of sophisticated machine learning when overwhelmed by dataset complexity. This leads to suboptimal decision-making and missed opportunities for learning from previous cycles.
AI offers several approaches to accelerate this process. Active learning strategies can replace large-scale screening with small batches of computationally designed compounds, similar to uncertainty sampling in machine learning where you only label the most informative examples. The key insight is that instead of testing millions of random compounds, you can use generative models to propose a few hundred carefully chosen candidates per cycle, dramatically reducing the synthesis burden.
The synthesis bottleneck itself could be addressed through AI-optimized reaction planning, essentially treating chemical synthesis as a combinatorial optimization problem. By predicting the most efficient synthetic routes and reaction conditions, AI could enable “right first time” synthesis, reducing the trial-and-error component that currently extends timelines. Laboratory automation combined with AI guidance could potentially compress the make phase from weeks to days.
A concrete example demonstrates both the promise and current limitations of this approach. Researchers used reinforcement learning to generate 30,000 virtual molecules, filtered them down to 6 candidates through various computational criteria, and successfully synthesized 2 compounds with strong biological activity - all in 46 days. However, the best compound turned out to be a minor chemical modification of known drugs, suggesting the AI primarily rediscovered existing knowledge rather than finding truly novel solutions.
The ultimate vision is a mostly virtual DMTA cycle where accurate predictive models eliminate most physical synthesis and testing, with only occasional validation experiments. This would transform drug discovery from a primarily experimental process to a primarily computational one, similar to how machine learning has shifted many domains from rule-based to data-driven approaches. However, this requires solving the fundamental data quality and model reliability problems outlined in previous challenges, plus developing robust methods for low-data situations where little prior knowledge exists about the biological target.
Research Culture and the Appropriate Mind-set
The biggest barrier to AI adoption in drug discovery isn’t technical but cultural. Success depends entirely on whether scientists, business stakeholders, and other domain experts are willing to trust, understand, and effectively integrate AI tools into their workflows. This is fundamentally a human-computer interaction problem disguised as a technical one.
The core challenge is bridging different “cultures” - communities that use different languages, methods, and exemplars. Computer scientists think in terms of loss functions and training sets, while medicinal chemists think in terms of molecular mechanisms and synthetic feasibility. Business stakeholders focus on timelines and risk management. These groups need to develop a common vocabulary and shared understanding of how AI fits into the drug discovery process, similar to how successful interdisciplinary ML projects require translating between domain expertise and technical implementation.
Three key drivers shape how this cultural integration will unfold. Personalization demands AI systems that can adapt to individual patients and disease variants, requiring models that can handle extreme heterogeneity and small patient populations. Automation pushes toward replacing manual processes with AI-driven pipelines, but this requires building trust in black-box systems making high-stakes decisions. Materialization focuses on the practical constraints of synthesizing and delivering drugs at scale, connecting computational predictions to physical manufacturing realities.
The most promising approach is positioning AI as augmentation rather than replacement. Instead of trying to automate chemists out of the process, AI should handle the tedious data curation and pattern recognition tasks that scientists find burdensome, freeing them to focus on creative problem-solving and domain insight. This creates a positive feedback loop where better human-curated data improves AI performance, which in turn provides more useful insights for human experts.
A critical technical requirement for adoption is interpretability. Scientists need to understand not just what the AI recommends, but why it made that recommendation. This goes beyond standard explainability techniques to require domain-specific explanations that connect AI outputs to chemical intuition and biological mechanisms. The AI system must be able to provide comprehensible rationales that allow experts to validate, critique, and build upon its suggestions.
The success of this integration depends on designing AI systems that can learn from human feedback and adapt their behavior based on expert input. Rather than treating the human as simply a user of the AI system, the framework should enable bidirectional learning where the AI observes and learns from human decision-making patterns while providing increasingly useful support. This requires moving beyond standard supervised learning toward more interactive learning paradigms that can handle partially defined objectives and incorporate expert knowledge throughout the process.
Ultimately, the goal is creating collaborative partnerships between human experts and AI systems, each contributing their unique strengths to solve problems neither could handle alone. This cultural shift requires viewing AI as a sophisticated tool that enhances human capability rather than a replacement technology that threatens existing expertise.

Introduction
Neural network quantization is a crucial technique for deploying deep learning models on resource-constrained devices. By reducing the precision of weights and activations from 32-bit floating-point to lower bit-width representations (such as 8-bit integers), quantization significantly decreases memory requirements and computational complexity while maintaining reasonable accuracy. This blogpost presents the mathematical foundation of neural network quantization along with a practical example on how this could be implemented in practice for a simple Convolution + BatchNorm + ReLU block!
Mathematical Foundation
Problem Statement
In neural network quantization, we aim to map values from a continuous floating-point domain to a discrete integer domain. Specifically:
We have a source distribution with values in range \([x_{\min}, x_{\max}]\)
We want to map to a target quantized range \([q_{\min}, q_{\max}]\)
Our goal is to find a linear quantization function defined by two parameters:
A scale factor \(s > 0\)
A zero-point value \(z \in \mathbb{Z}\) within the range \([q_{\min}, q_{\max}]\)
Such that the quantization operation:
\[q = \text{clamp}\left(\lfloor{\frac{x}{s} + z}\rceil,\  q_{\min},\  q_{\max}\right)\]
And the dequantization operation:
\[\hat{x} = (q - z) \times s\]
Together minimize the quantization error \(|x - \hat{x}|\) across the distribution of values.
Asymmetric quantization
Asymmetric quantization is a technique where the zero value in our original floating-point representation doesn’t necessarily map to zero in our quantized representation.
For a mapping that preserves the full original floating point domain’s dynamic range, we want the extremes of our floating-point range to correspond to the extremes of our quantized range:
\(x_{\min}\) should map approximately to \(q_{\min}\)
\(x_{\max}\) should map approximately to \(q_{\max}\)
We can then derive the scale factor by setting up the following equations (ignoring rounding for now):
For the minimum value:
\[q_{\min} = \frac{x_{\min}}{s} + z\]
For the maximum value:
\[q_{\max} = \frac{x_{\max}}{s} + z\]
Subtracting these equations:
\[q_{\max} - q_{\min} = \frac{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}{s}\]
Solving for \(s\):
\[s = \frac{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}{q_{\max} - q_{\min}}\]
This scale factor represents the “step size” in the original floating-point domain that corresponds to an increment of 1 in the quantized domain.
Using our derived scale factor, we can solve for the zero-point \(z\):
\[z = q_{\min} - \frac{x_{\min}}{s}\]
Substituting our expression for \(s\):
\[z = q_{\min} - \frac{x_{\min}(q_{\max} - q_{\min})}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}\]
Since \(z\) must be an integer, we round the result:
\[z = \left\lfloor q_{\min} - \frac{x_{\min}(q_{\max} - q_{\min})}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}} \right\rceil\]
Finally, we clamp \(z\) to ensure it stays within the quantized range:
\[z = \text{clamp}(z, q_{\min}, q_{\max})\]
Asymmetric Quantization AnimationSymmetric Quantization
Keeping in mind that most neural network weight and activation distributions are concentrated near zero, we often prefer to apply symmetric quantization around zero, meaning that we want to force the 0.0 value in our original distribution to map to 0 (or 128) in our quantized distribution.
Symmetric quantization prioritizes computational efficiency over perfect range utilization. It deliberately sacrifices some representational capacity to gain significant benefits.
The computational benefits of symmetric quantization include:
Simplified multiplication: \((q_1 - z) \times (q_2 - z)\) becomes just \(q_1 \times q_2\) when \(z=0\) (if we are using signed integer representations)
Hardware acceleration: Many NPUs and DSPs are optimized for symmetric quantization
Better numerical properties: Exact representation of zero prevents bias accumulation
In this case we start by fixing the zero point:
For signed integers (e.g., INT8 with \(q_{\min}=-128\) and \(q_{\max}=127\)):
\[z = 0\]
For unsigned integers (e.g., UINT8 with \(q_{\min}=0\) and \(q_{\max}=255\)):
\[z = \frac{q_{\max} + q_{\min}}{2} = 128\]
The scale can then be calculated in multiple ways, for example:
\[s = \frac{\max(|x_{\min}|, |x_{\max}|)}{q_{\max} - z}\]
This ensures that floating-point zero maps exactly to the zero-point in the quantized domain.
Symmetric Quantization - Min-Max dynamic rangeInstead of picking \(\max(|x_{\min}|, |x_{\max}|)\) to compute the scale parameters, we can:
Use percentile-based clipping (e.g., 0.1% and 99.9%) to exclude extreme outliers
Apply KL-divergence minimization to find optimal quantization ranges that preserve the information content
Use MSE (Mean Squared Error) minimization between original and quantized values
Employ calibration sets to determine optimal quantization parameters dynamically during inference
These approaches better preserve the important regions of the distribution while still maintaining the computational benefits of symmetric quantization.
Symmetric Quantization - 95% percentile dynamic rangeConvolution Example
When quantizing a neural network, it’s crucial to understand how convolution operations are implemented computationally. One common approach in deep learning frameworks is to use a technique called Im2Col (image-to-column) that transforms convolutions into General Matrix Multiply (GEMM) operations. While the actual hardware implementation may vary (some NPUs use direct convolution or other optimizations), understanding the im2col transformation provides valuable insight into quantization mechanics.
Let’s work through a complete example: consider a 3×3 convolution kernel applied to a 4×4 input image (no padding).
We define the input image and kernel as:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{X} \in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 4} &= \begin{bmatrix}
x_{0} & x_{1} & x_{2} & x_{3} \\
x_{4} & x_{5} & x_{6} & x_{7} \\
x_{8} & x_{9} & x_{10} & x_{11} \\
x_{12} & x_{13} & x_{14} & x_{15}
\end{bmatrix}
\\
\mathbf{K} \in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3} &= \begin{bmatrix}
k_{0} & k_{1} & k_{2} \\
k_{3} & k_{4} & k_{5} \\
k_{6} & k_{7} & k_{8}
\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
\]
The Im2Col Transformation
We use Im2Col to extract overlapping patches from the input image. Each column in the resulting matrix contains the input values that interact with one application of the kernel.
For our 4×4 input with a 3×3 kernel, we get four 3×3 patches (one for each output position). We flatten each patch into a column vector:
\[
\mathbf{X}_{\text{im2col}} = \begin{bmatrix}
x_{0} & x_{1} & x_{4} & x_{5} \\
x_{1} & x_{2} & x_{5} & x_{6} \\
x_{2} & x_{3} & x_{6} & x_{7} \\
x_{4} & x_{5} & x_{8} & x_{9} \\
x_{5} & x_{6} & x_{9} & x_{10} \\
x_{6} & x_{7} & x_{10} & x_{11} \\
x_{8} & x_{9} & x_{12} & x_{13} \\
x_{9} & x_{10} & x_{13} & x_{14} \\
x_{10} & x_{11} & x_{14} & x_{15}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
We also flatten the kernel into a row vector:
\[
\mathbf{k}^T = \begin{bmatrix} k_{0} & k_{1} & k_{2} & k_{3} & k_{4} & k_{5} & k_{6} & k_{7} & k_{8} \end{bmatrix}
\]
The convolution then becomes a simple matrix-vector multiplication:
\[
\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{k}^T \mathbf{X}_{\text{im2col}} + \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix}y_0 & y_1 & y_2 & y_3\end{bmatrix}
\]
which gives us the vectorized 2×2 output feature map that can be reshaped as:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}y_0 & y_1 & y_2 & y_3\end{bmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{bmatrix}
y_0 & y_1 \\
y_2 & y_3
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Quantized Matrix Multiplication Mathematics
Now we derive how quantized matrix multiplication theory applies to a generic matrix operation \(\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{B}\). We’ll use our established notation where quantized tensors have subscript \(q\) and each tensor has its own scale (\(s\)) and zero-point (\(z\)) parameters.
Suggestion: try to read this chapter without thinking of convolutions, let’s keep it as generic as possible!
Let’s denote:
\(\color{red}{\mathbf{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_X \times C_X}\)
\(\color{red}{\mathbf{X}_q}\): quantized \(\mathbf{X}\) matrix with scale \(s_X\) and zero-point \(z_X\)
\(\color{blue}{\mathbf{W}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_W \times C_W}\)
\(\color{blue}{\mathbf{W}_q}\): quantized \(\mathbf{W}\) matrix with scale \(s_W\) and zero-point \(z_W\)
\(\color{purple}{\mathbf{B}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_W \times C_X}\)
\(\color{purple}{\mathbf{B}_q}\): quantized \(\mathbf{B}\) matrix with scale \(s_B\) and zero-point \(z_B\)
\(\color{green}{\mathbf{Y}_q}\): quantized output matrix with scale \(s_Y\) and zero-point \(z_Y\)
\(\color{green}{\mathbf{Y}_q}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_W \times C_X}\)
\(C_W = N_X\)
From the dequantization formula, we can write each floating-point value as:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\color{red}{X_{j,k}} &= s_X(\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k} - z_X) \\
\color{blue}{W_{i,j}} &= s_W(\mathbf{W}_{q,i,j} - z_W) \\
\color{purple}{B_{i,k}} &= s_B(\mathbf{B}_{q,i,k} - z_B) \\
\color{green}{Y_{i,k}} &= s_Y(\mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k} - z_Y)
\end{aligned}
\]
The \((i,k)\)-th element of our matrix multiplication output is:
\[
Y_{i,k} = \sum_{j=1}^{C_W}\left(W_{i,j} \cdot X_{j,k}\right) + B_{i,k}
\]
Substituting our dequantization expressions:
\[
Y_{i,k} = \sum_{j=1}^{C_W}\left( \color{blue}{s_W(\mathbf{W}_{q,i,j} - z_W)} \cdot \color{red}{s_X(\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k} - z_X)}\right) + \color{purple}{s_B(\mathbf{B}_{q,i,k} - z_B)}
\]
\[
Y_{i,k} = s_X s_W \sum_{j=1}^{C_W}\left( (\mathbf{W}_{q,i,j} - z_W)(\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k} - z_X)\right) + s_B(\mathbf{B}_{q,i,k} - z_B)
\]
Expanding the product inside the sum:
\[
Y_{i,k} = s_X s_W \sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \left[\mathbf{W}_{q,i,j}\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k} - z_W\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k} - z_X\mathbf{W}_{q,i,j} + z_X z_W\right] + s_B(\mathbf{B}_{q,i,k} - z_B)
\]
\[
Y_{i,k} = s_X s_W \left[\sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{W}_{q,i,j}\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k} - z_W\sum_{j=1}^{C_W}\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k} - z_X\sum_{j=1}^{C_W}\mathbf{W}_{q,i,j} + C_W \cdot z_X z_W\right] + s_B(\mathbf{B}_{q,i,k} - z_B)
\]
Since \(\color{green}{Y_{i,k}} = s_Y(\mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k} - z_Y)\), we can solve for the quantized output:
\[
s_Y(\mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k} - z_Y) = s_X s_W \left[\sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{W}_{q,i,j}\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k} - z_W\sum_{j=1}^{C_W}\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k} - z_X\sum_{j=1}^{C_W}\mathbf{W}_{q,i,j} + C_W \cdot z_X z_W\right] + s_B(\mathbf{B}_{q,i,k} - z_B)
\]
Defining the multiplier \(M := \frac{s_X s_W}{s_Y}\) and rearranging:
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k} = z_Y + M \left[
\color{blue}{\sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{W}_{q,i,j}\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k}}
-
z_W\color{red}{\sum_{j=1}^{C_W}\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k}} -
z_X\color{orange}{\sum_{j=1}^{C_W}\mathbf{W}_{q,i,j}} + C_W \cdot z_X z_W\right] + \frac{s_B}{s_Y}(\mathbf{B}_{q,i,k} - z_B)
}
\]
We can further define:
\(\color{red}{a_k^{(X)} := \sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{X}_{q,j,k}}\)
\(\color{orange}{\bar{a}_i^{(W)} := \sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{W}_{q,i,j}}\)
This gives us the final form:
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k} = z_Y + M \left[
\color{blue}{\sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{W}_{q,i,j}\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k}}
-
z_W\color{red}{a_k^{(X)}} -
z_X\color{orange}{\bar{a}_i^{(W)}} + C_W \cdot z_X z_W\right] + \frac{s_B}{s_Y}(\mathbf{B}_{q,i,k} - z_B)
}
\]
Computational Complexity Analysis
Keeping in mind that the final output \(\color{green}{\mathbf{Y}_q}\in\mathbb{R}^{\color{purple}{N_W \times C_X}}\)
, we will now inspect the computational cost breakdown:
Constant / pre-computable terms
To make our life easier, let’s first check what can actually be pre-computed from our quantized matrix multiplication formula, assuming that \(\mathbf{B}\) and \(\mathbf{W}\) are known at compile-time (as it’s the case for machine-learning applications). Let’s color the pre-computable terms in gray:
\[
\mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k} = \color{gray}{M \cdot C_W \cdot z_X z_W + z_Y + M} \color{blue}{\sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{W}_{q,i,j}\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k}} - \color{gray}{M \cdot z_W} \cdot \color{red}{a_k^{(X)}} - \color{gray}{M \cdot z_X\bar{a}_i^{(W)}} + \color{gray}{\frac{s_B}{s_Y}(\mathbf{B}_{q,i,k} - z_B)}
\]
Rearranging,
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k} = \color{gray}{M} \color{blue}{\sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{W}_{q,i,j}\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k}} - \color{gray}{M^{'}} \cdot \color{red}{a_k^{(X)}} + \color{gray}{\gamma_{i,k}}  
}
\]
Where:
\[
\color{gray}{\gamma_{i,k}} = \frac{s_B}{s_Y}(\mathbf{B}_{q,i,k} - z_B) + M \cdot C_W \cdot z_X z_W + z_Y - M \cdot z_X\bar{a}_i^{(W)}\\
\color{gray}{M^{'}} = M \cdot z_W
\]
Let’s now see what the actual run-time time complexity is.
First, we need to compute \(\color{red}{a_k^{(X)} = \sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{X}_{q,j,k}}\) for all \(k\)s (i.e. for \(C_X\) times), this requires \((C_W - 1)\times C_X\) additions.
Afterwards, for each \(\mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k}\) we need to compute:
\(\color{blue}{\sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{W}_{q,i,j}\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k}}\), which requires \(\left(C_W - 1\right)\) additions and \(C_W\) multiplications).
\(2\) multiplications (the ones involving \(\color{gray}{M}\) and \(\color{gray}{M^{'}}\))
\(2\) additions (the final accumulations for \(-\color{gray}{M^{'}} \cdot \color{red}{a_k^{(X)}} + \color{gray}{\gamma_{i,k}}\))
So, remembering that \(\color{green}{\mathbf{Y}_q}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_W \times C_X}\), the total number of operations can be calculated as:
\[
\boxed{(C_W - 1)\times C_X + \color{green}{N_W \times C_X}\times\left(C_W - 1 + 2\right)}\ \ \ \text{additions}\\
\boxed{\color{green}{N_W \times C_X}\times\left(C_W +2\right)}\ \ \ \text{multiplications}\\
\]
The total complexity is dominated by the core matrix multiplication term when \(C_W\) is reasonably large, and the core computation scales as \(O(N_W \times C_X \times C_W)\).
Applying the Complexity Analysis to Convolutions
Now that we’ve derived the computational complexity for generic quantized matrix multiplication, let’s see how this translates to actual convolution operations.
Understanding the Im2Col Dimension Transformation
Before we can map the complexity formulas, we need to understand how the im2col transformation changes our tensor dimensions.
Consider a convolution operation with the following parameters:
\(K_H\), \(K_W\): kernel height and width
\(C_{in}\): number of input channels
\(C_{out}\): number of output channels
\(H_{in}\), \(W_{in}\): input feature map height and width
\(H_{out}\), \(W_{out}\): output feature map height and width
The original input tensor \(\mathbf{X}\) has shape \((C_{in}, H_{in}, W_{in})\). However, the im2col transformation extracts overlapping patches and reshapes them into a 2D matrix \(\mathbf{X}_{\text{im2col}}\) with dimensions:
\[
\mathbf{X}_{\text{im2col}} \in \mathbb{R}^{(K_H \cdot K_W \cdot C_{in}) \times (H_{out} \cdot W_{out})}
\]
Each column of \(\mathbf{X}_{\text{im2col}}\) contains one flattened receptive field patch (of size \(K_H \times K_W \times C_{in}\)), and we have \(H_{out} \times W_{out}\) such patches—one for each output spatial position.
Similarly, the weight tensor is reshaped from \((C_{out}, C_{in}, K_H, K_W)\) into:
\[
\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{C_{out} \times (K_H \cdot K_W \cdot C_{in})}
\]
The convolution then becomes the matrix multiplication \(\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{W} \mathbf{X}_{\text{im2col}}\), where \(\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{C_{out} \times (H_{out} \cdot W_{out})}\).
Mapping to Generic Matrix Multiplication Variables
The following table maps our generic matrix multiplication variables to their convolution-specific interpretations:
Generic Variable
Convolution Equivalent
Description
\(N_W\)
\(C_{out}\)
Number of output channels (rows of \(\mathbf{W}\))
\(C_W\)
\(K_H \cdot K_W \cdot C_{in}\)
Receptive field size (columns of \(\mathbf{W}\))
\(N_X\)
\(K_H \cdot K_W \cdot C_{in}\)
Rows of \(\mathbf{X}_{\text{im2col}}\) (matches \(C_W\))
\(C_X\)
\(H_{out} \cdot W_{out}\)
Number of output spatial positions (columns of \(\mathbf{X}_{\text{im2col}}\))
Substituting these convolution-specific dimensions into our complexity formulas, we get:
\[
\boxed{(K_H \cdot K_W \cdot C_{in} - 1) \times (H_{out} \cdot W_{out}) + C_{out} \times (H_{out} \cdot W_{out}) \times (K_H \cdot K_W \cdot C_{in} + 1)}\ \ \ \text{additions}
\]
\[
\boxed{C_{out} \times (H_{out} \cdot W_{out}) \times (K_H \cdot K_W \cdot C_{in} + 2)}\ \ \ \text{multiplications}
\]
For a typical 3×3 convolution with 64 input channels, 128 output channels, and a 56×56 output spatial size:
Additions: \(\approx 1.46\) billion operations
Multiplications: \(\approx 2.61\) billion operations
The dominant computational term is \(C_{out} \times H_{out} \times W_{out} \times K_H \times K_W \times C_{in}\), which represents the core convolution computation.
ReLU Example
Introduction
The Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) is one of the most widely used activation functions in deep neural networks. While the standard ReLU function is typically defined as \(\max(0, x)\), for quantization purposes, it’s beneficial to work with a more generalized form that provides greater flexibility and clearer mathematical derivation.
Generalized ReLU Function
We define a generalized ReLU activation function as:
\[
\text{ReLU}(x, a, b, c) = \begin{cases}
a & \text{if } x < b \\
a + c(x - b) & \text{if } x \geq b
\end{cases}
\]
Where:
\(a\) represents the output value for the inactive region (when \(x < b\))
\(b\) is the threshold point where the activation switches from inactive to active
\(c\) is the slope of the active region (when \(x \geq b\))
This generalized form encompasses the Standard ReLU formulation as \(\text{ReLU}(x, 0, 0, 1)\).
Derivation of Quantized ReLU
As usual, let’s denote:
\(x_q\): quantized input
\(y_q\): quantized output
\(s_x\), \(z_x\): scale and zero-point for input quantization
\(s_y\), \(z_y\): scale and zero-point for output quantization
Let’s derive the quantized ReLU step by step, starting with the standard ReLU case where \(a = 0\), \(b = 0\), and \(c = 1\).
We begin with the standard ReLU function:
\[
y = \text{ReLU}(x, 0, 0, 1) = \begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } x < 0 \\
x & \text{if } x \geq 0
\end{cases}
\]
Using the quantization relationships:
\[
y = s_y(y_q - z_y)
\]
Substituting this into our ReLU function:
\[
s_y(y_q - z_y) = \begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } x < 0 \\
x & \text{if } x \geq 0
\end{cases}
\]
Dividing both sides by \(s_y\):
\[
y_q - z_y = \begin{cases}
0/s_y & \text{if } x < 0 \\
x/s_y & \text{if } x \geq 0
\end{cases}
\]
Therefore:
\[
y_q =  \begin{cases}
z_y & \text{if } x < 0 \\
z_y +x/s_y & \text{if } x \geq 0
\end{cases}
\]
Now we substitute \(x = s_x(x_q - z_x)\):
\[
y_q = \begin{cases}
z_y  & \text{if } s_x(x_q - z_x) < 0 \\
z_y + s_x(x_q - z_x)/s_y & \text{if } s_x(x_q - z_x) \geq 0
\end{cases}
\]
Since \(s_x > 0\) (scale is always positive), the condition \(s_x(x_q - z_x) < 0\) is equivalent to \(x_q - z_x < 0\), or \(x_q < z_x\).
Therefore:
\[
y_q = \begin{cases}
z_y & \text{if } x_q < z_x \\
z_y + \frac{s_x}{s_y}(x_q - z_x) & \text{if } x_q \geq z_x
\end{cases}
\]
This can be expressed as a generalized ReLU in quantized space:
\[
y_q = \text{ReLU}\left(x_q, z_y, z_x, \frac{s_x}{s_y}\right)
\]
Batch Normalization in Quantized Networks
Batch Normalization (BatchNorm) is ubiquitous in modern neural networks, but it presents unique challenges in quantized inference. The good news is that during inference, BatchNorm can often be completely eliminated through a technique called weight folding or BatchNorm fusion. Understanding this process is crucial for real hardware deployment, as it directly impacts memory usage, computational efficiency, and numerical stability.
Mathematical Foundation of Batch Normalization
Batch normalization applies the following transformation to each feature map channel:
\[
y = \frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} \cdot \gamma + \beta
\]
Where:
\(x\) is the input feature map
\(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) are the running mean and variance (computed during training)
\(\epsilon\) is a small constant for numerical stability (typically \(10^{-5}\))
\(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) are learnable scale and shift parameters
During inference, \(\mu\), \(\sigma^2\), \(\gamma\), and \(\beta\) are all fixed constants.
The Challenge with Quantized BatchNorm
If we naively apply quantized BatchNorm, we’d need to:
Dequantize the input: \(x = s_{in}(x_q - z_{in})\)
Apply BatchNorm in floating-point
Quantize the output: \(y_q = \text{round}(y/s_{out}) + z_{out}\)
This approach is problematic because:
Multiple quantization steps introduce cumulative errors.
Floating-point operations defeat the purpose of quantization.
Memory overhead from storing multiple sets of quantization parameters.
BatchNorm Folding
The key insight is that during inference, BatchNorm is just an affine transformation that can be absorbed into the preceding convolution layer.
Step 1: Rewrite BatchNorm as Affine Transform
First, let’s simplify the BatchNorm formula
\[
y = \frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} \cdot \gamma + \beta = x\cdot\color{blue}{\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}}} \color{red}{- \frac{\mu\cdot\gamma}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} + \beta}
\]
by defining:
\[
\color{blue}\alpha = \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} \quad \text{and} \quad \color{red}\phi = \beta - \frac{\mu \cdot \gamma}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}}
\]
Then BatchNorm becomes:
\[
y = \alpha \cdot x + \phi
\]
Step 2: Fold into Convolution Weights
Consider a convolution followed by BatchNorm:
\[
\begin{aligned}
z &= \text{Conv}(x, W, b) = W \star x + b \\
y &= \text{BatchNorm}(z) = \alpha \cdot z + \phi
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting the convolution output:
\[
y = \alpha \cdot (W \star x + b) + \phi = (\alpha \cdot W) \star x + (\alpha \cdot b + \phi)
\]
This gives us the folded parameters:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
W_{\text{folded}} &= \alpha \cdot W \\
b_{\text{folded}} &= \alpha \cdot b + \phi
\end{aligned}
}
\]
Step 3: Quantize the Folded Layer
Now we quantize the folded convolution layer directly using our standard quantization formulas, completely eliminating the separate BatchNorm operation.
Derivation of Quantized Conv+BatchNorm+ReLU
Let’s derive the complete fused operation step by step, carefully tracking how BatchNorm folding affects our quantization parameters.
From our earlier derivation, the quantized matrix multiplication for element \((i,k)\) is:
\[
\mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k} = z_Y + M \left[
\sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{W}_{q,i,j}\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k}
- z_W \sum_{j=1}^{C_W}\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k}
- z_X \sum_{j=1}^{C_W}\mathbf{W}_{q,i,j}
+ C_W \cdot z_X z_W
\right] + \frac{s_B}{s_Y}(\mathbf{B}_{q,i,k} - z_B)
\]
Where \(M = \frac{s_X s_W}{s_Y}\) is the scale multiplier.
After folding BatchNorm into the convolution, we have:
\[
\mathbf{W}_{\text{folded}} = \alpha \cdot \mathbf{W} \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{b}_{\text{folded}} = \alpha \cdot \mathbf{b} + \phi
\]
Where \(\alpha = \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}}\) and \(\phi = \beta - \frac{\mu \cdot \gamma}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}}\).
Important: The folded weights have a different distribution than the original weights, so we must recompute the quantization parameters:
\(s_{W_{\text{folded}}}\): scale for quantized folded weights
\(z_{W_{\text{folded}}}\): zero-point for quantized folded weights
\(s_{b_{\text{folded}}}\): scale for quantized folded bias
\(z_{b_{\text{folded}}}\): zero-point for quantized folded bias
Replacing \(\mathbf{W}\) with \(\mathbf{W}_{\text{folded}}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) with \(\mathbf{b}_{\text{folded}}\) in our quantized convolution formula:
\[
\mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k} = z_Y + M_{\text{folded}} \left[
\sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{W}_{\text{folded},q,i,j}\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k}
- z_{W_{\text{folded}}} \sum_{j=1}^{C_W}\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k}
- z_X \sum_{j=1}^{C_W}\mathbf{W}_{\text{folded},q,i,j}
+ C_W \cdot z_X z_{W_{\text{folded}}}
\right] + \frac{s_{b_{\text{folded}}}}{s_Y}(\mathbf{b}_{\text{folded},q,i} - z_{b_{\text{folded}}})
\]
Where the new multiplier is:
\[
M_{\text{folded}} = \frac{s_X s_{W_{\text{folded}}}}{s_Y}
\]
We can simplify using the aggregation terms from earlier:
\(a_k^{(X)} = \sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{X}_{q,j,k}\)
\(\bar{a}_i^{(W_{\text{folded}})} = \sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{W}_{\text{folded},q,i,j}\)
Giving us:
\[
\mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k} = z_Y + M_{\text{folded}} \left[
\sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{W}_{\text{folded},q,i,j}\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k}
- z_{W_{\text{folded}}} a_k^{(X)}
- z_X \bar{a}_i^{(W_{\text{folded}})}
+ C_W \cdot z_X z_{W_{\text{folded}}}
\right] + \frac{s_{b_{\text{folded}}}}{s_Y}(\mathbf{b}_{\text{folded},q,i} - z_{b_{\text{folded}}})
\]
From our earlier ReLU derivation, we know that for standard ReLU (\(a=0, b=0, c=1\)), the quantized form is:
\[
\text{output}_q = \begin{cases}
z_{\text{out}} & \text{if } \mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k} < z_Y \\
z_{\text{out}} + \frac{s_Y}{s_{\text{out}}}(\mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k} - z_Y) & \text{if } \mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k} \geq z_Y
\end{cases}
\]
Or equivalently, using our generalized ReLU notation:
\[
\boxed{
\text{output}_q = \text{ReLU}\left(\mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k},\ z_{\text{out}},\ z_Y,\ \frac{s_Y}{s_{\text{out}}}\right)
}
\]
Note that:
The threshold is \(z_Y\) (the zero-point of the pre-activation)
The inactive value is \(z_{\text{out}}\) (the zero-point of the output)
The slope is \(\frac{s_Y}{s_{\text{out}}}\) (the ratio of scales)
If we choose our quantization parameters such that \(s_Y = s_{\text{out}}\) (same scale before and after ReLU), the slope becomes 1, simplifying the operation.
Complete Fused Operation
The complete Conv+BatchNorm+ReLU fusion in quantized arithmetic:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k} &= z_Y + M_{\text{folded}} \left[
\sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{W}_{\text{folded},q,i,j}\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k}
- z_{W_{\text{folded}}} a_k^{(X)}
- z_X \bar{a}_i^{(W_{\text{folded}})}
+ C_W \cdot z_X z_{W_{\text{folded}}}
\right] \\
&\quad + \frac{s_{b_{\text{folded}}}}{s_Y}(\mathbf{b}_{\text{folded},q,i} - z_{b_{\text{folded}}}) \\[1em]
\text{output}_{q,i,k} &= \text{ReLU}\left(\mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k},\ z_{\text{out}},\ z_Y,\ \frac{s_Y}{s_{\text{out}}}\right)
\end{aligned}
}
\]
Where:
\(a_k^{(X)} = \sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{X}_{q,j,k}\) (sum over input columns, can be precomputed)
\(\bar{a}_i^{(W_{\text{folded}})} = \sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{W}_{\text{folded},q,i,j}\) (sum over weight rows, precomputed at compile-time)
\(M_{\text{folded}} = \frac{s_X s_{W_{\text{folded}}}}{s_Y}\) (precomputed multiplier)
Following our earlier complexity analysis approach, we can consolidate out implementation-ready as:
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k} = \color{gray}{M_{\text{folded}}} \color{blue}{\sum_{j=1}^{C_W} \mathbf{W}_{\text{folded},q,i,j}\mathbf{X}_{q,j,k}} - \color{gray}{M_{\text{folded}}^{'}} \color{red}{a_k^{(X)}} + \color{gray}{\gamma_i}
}
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
\color{gray}{M_{\text{folded}}^{'}} &= M_{\text{folded}} \cdot z_{W_{\text{folded}}} = \frac{s_X s_{W_{\text{folded}}}}{s_Y} \cdot z_{W_{\text{folded}}} \\[0.5em]
\color{gray}{\gamma_{i}} &= z_Y + M_{\text{folded}} \cdot C_W \cdot z_X z_{W_{\text{folded}}} - M_{\text{folded}} \cdot z_X \cdot \bar{a}_i^{(W_{\text{folded}})} + \frac{s_{b_{\text{folded}}}}{s_Y}(\mathbf{b}_{\text{folded},q,i} - z_{b_{\text{folded}}})
\end{aligned}
\]
ReLU Simplification
For the ReLU operation, if we choose \(s_Y = s_{\text{out}}\) and \(z_Y = z_{\text{out}}\), the quantized ReLU simplifies dramatically:
\[
\text{output}_{q,i,k} = \max(\mathbf{Y}_{q,i,k}, z_{\text{out}})
\]
This is just a simple comparison and clamp operation with zero additional multiplications or floating-point operations!
Appendix: On Scale and Zero-Point Matching in ReLU. (todo: clean-up!!!)
In our derivation of the fused Conv+BatchNorm+ReLU operation, we mentioned the simplification that occurs when \(s_Y = s_{\text{out}}\) and \(z_Y = z_{\text{out}}\). This deserves clarification, as it represents a common design decision in quantized inference.
The Calibration Question
During typical quantization calibration, separate quantization parameters would be computed for:
Pre-ReLU outputs (\(s_Y\), \(z_Y\)): based on the distribution before the activation
Post-ReLU outputs (\(s_{\text{out}}\), \(z_{\text{out}}\)): based on the distribution after ReLU clips negative values
These distributions differ since the the pre-ReLU range includes negative values that ReLU zeros out. Using different parameters would theoretically allow optimal quantization of each distribution.
The Practical Tradeoff
However, most modern quantization frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow Lite, ONNX Runtime) employ operator fusion where Conv+ReLU (or Conv+BN+ReLU) become a single fused operation. In this approach:
Only the post-ReLU distribution is calibrated to obtain \(s_{\text{out}}\) and \(z_{\text{out}}\)
These same parameters are used for the pre-ReLU values: \(s_Y = s_{\text{out}}\) and \(z_Y = z_{\text{out}}\)
The ReLU becomes a simple integer comparison: \(\text{output}_q = \max(\mathbf{Y}_{q}, z_{\text{out}})\)
This eliminates the need for dequantization → float ReLU → requantization, replacing it with pure integer operations.
Cost: Sub-optimal quantization of pre-ReLU values (quantization bins are wasted on the negative range that gets clipped).
Benefit: Zero floating-point operations, simpler hardware implementation, no cumulative quantization error.
For ReLU specifically, this tradeoff is favorable because negative values are discarded anyway, making the precision loss minimal while the computational savings are substantial. This is why operator fusion with scale matching is the standard practice in production quantization pipelines.
Real world example
The need for 32-bit accumulation
Before diving into a real world example with Python snippets showing how a convolution + ReLU activation would be carried out, we need to understand why proper accumulation is essential for quantized operations.
The fundamental issue is arithmetic overflow during the accumulation process.
Consider a typical convolution scenario: we’re multiplying int8 values (range: -128 to 127) and accumulating the results. Each multiplication can produce values up to 127 × 127 = 16,129. In a 3×3 convolution, we perform 9 such multiplications, potentially reaching 145,161. A larger 5×5 kernel could reach 403,225. These values far exceed the int8 range (-128 to 127) and even the int16 range (-32,768 to 32,767).
The solution is a three-stage accumulation strategy:
Computation Stage: Multiply int8 × int8 values, but accumulate in int32 registers
Correction Stage: Apply scale factors and zero-point corrections in float32 for precision
Output Stage: Quantize the result back to int8 for the next layer
This approach maintains numerical stability while preserving the computational efficiency of int8 operations. Modern AI accelerators are specifically designed around this pattern, with dedicated int8 multiply-accumulate units that output to int32 registers.

Introduction
The seminal paper “Attention Is All You Need” by Vaswani et al. quietly revolutionised the world of AI when it appeared in 2017. Little did its authors know they were laying the foundations for the creation of today’s Large Language Models, along with AI’s entrance into the mainstream. But before all that chaos, there was just this elegant idea about attention mechanisms that genuinely changed everything.
Why is this paper important?
The work presented in the paper was initially conceived to find a more efficient and performant solution to the problem of sequence-to-sequence modeling, a machine learning task that involves converting an input sequence into an output sequence, potentially of different lengths. The experiments from the paper presented results for English-to-German and English-to-French translation tasks. The state-of-the-art solutions at the time relied mainly on complex building blocks such as Recurrent Neural Networks and Convolutional Neural Networks, along with attention mechanisms first introduced in the 2014 paper “Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate” (Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio). The main hypothesis, as the title of the paper states, is that “Attention is all you need,” and by introducing a novel architecture called the Transformer, which exclusively leverages highly parallelizable and efficient attention mechanisms, it is possible to achieve state-of-the-art results on machine translation tasks without using recurrence or convolution.
Background
Tokenization and Embedding
Before trying to understand the inner workings of the Transformer architecture you should be familiar with a couple of preprocessing operations needed in order to feed text to a neural network. Here we will introduce some lexical terms that you will find all over the literature so, if you are a beginner in the field, take your time to digest this section.
Let’s say we have an input sentence such as “Manuscripts don’t burn.”, this text has to be converted into an input sequence composed of multiple tokens, this procedure is called tokenization. A token can be a word, or a sub-word, depending on the tokenization technique (Byte-Pair Encoding in this case, but we will not further discuss it in this blog post).
“Manuscripts don’t burn.” → [“Man”, ”uscript”, “s”, “ don”, “’t”, “ burn”]
Here the original text was sub-divided in 6 tokens. We have a fixed number of possible tokens, which represents the cardinality of our dictionary \(\mathscr{D}\) ( e.g., in the paper a shared vocabulary of 37000 tokens was used for the English-to-German translation experiments, and a shared vocabulary of 32000 tokens was used for the English-to-French translation experiments). Once we have our tokens, we will map each token into a randomly initialised vector \(x\) of dimension \(d_{\text{model}}\), we call these vectors embeddings.
\[
x_{\text{(Man)}},\ x_{\text{(uscript)}},\ x_{\text{(s)}},\ x_{\text{( don)}},\ x_{\text{('t)}},\ x_{\text{( burn)}} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}
\]
Positional Encoding
Given that the Transformer architecture aims to process all tokens in parallel, and these randomly initialized embeddings contain no information regarding the position of the tokens in the sentence (we would like the model to be able to distinguish between “Manuscripts don’t burn” and ” don’t burn Manuscripts”), we add a positional encoding vector to each embeddding vector to obtain the final input embeddings.
\[
\textbf{x}_1 = \textbf{x}_{\text{(Man)}}  + \textbf{p}_{1} \\
\textbf{x}_2 = \textbf{x}_{\text{(uscript)}} + \textbf{p}_{2}  \\
\textbf{x}_3 = \textbf{x}_{\text{(s)}} + \textbf{p}_{3}  \\
\textbf{x}_4 = \textbf{x}_{\text{( don)}} + \textbf{p}_{4}  \\
\textbf{x}_5 = \textbf{x}_{\text{('t)}} + \textbf{p}_{5}  \\
\textbf{x}_6 = \textbf{x}_{\text{( burn)}}  + \textbf{p}_{6}
\]
We obtain these positional encoding vectors in the following way:
\[
\textbf{p}_{i} = f(i) \\ \\
f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}\\ \\
f(i)_{k}:=
\begin{Bmatrix}
\sin\left(w_k\cdot i\right) \ \ \ \ \text{if $k$ is even}\\
\cos\left(w_k\cdot i\right) \ \ \ \ \text{if $k$ is odd}\ \
\end{Bmatrix}\ \
w_k = \frac{1}{10000^{\frac{2k}{d_{\text{model}}}}}
\]
Just for completeness:
\[
\textbf{p}_{i} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\sin\left(w_0\cdot i\right)\\
\cos\left(w_0\cdot i\right)\\
\sin\left(w_1\cdot i\right)\\
\cos\left(w_1\cdot i\right)\\
\cdots \\
\sin\left(w_{d_{\text{model}}/2}\cdot i\right)\\
\cos\left(w_{d_{\text{model}}/2}\cdot i\right)
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Here is a visualization of how these positional embeddings would look like for the first \(1024\) embeddings where \(d_{\text{model}}=256\)




After reading this section you may already have many questions like:
Why are we adding these positional encodings to the randomly initialized embedding vectors instead of concatenating them?
Why was this formulation chosen over other ones? Does it have any desirable properties?
Is this still the chosen method to enforce position information in the input embeddings as today (2025)?
But this would require a separate blog post, so I’m asking you to proceed with this article without questioning the validity of such positional encodings.
Attention Mechanism
For simplicity, throughout this blog post, we’ll assume that each word in a sentence corresponds to a different token. Keep in mind that in practice, tokenization is more complex.
In the following sections, all vectors are represented as lowercase bold and are considered to be column vectors.
Scaled Dot Product Attention
Let’s develop an intuition about the most important building block of the entire architecture: the scaled dot-product attention mechanism. This component allows each word embedding to pay attention to surrounding words (its context) and update itself to better represent its true semantic meaning.
Consider these two example sentences:
“I want to wear my \(\color{brown}{\text{cool}}\) jacket”
“Today the weather is quite \(\color{blue}{\text{cool}}\)”
Before training the model the two word-embeddings for the word cool would be the same, even though they carry a well distinct meaning. As humans we understand that \(\color{brown}{\text{cool}}\) in the first sentence means “fashionable”, since it’s juxtaposed to the word “jacket”; and \(\color{blue}{\text{cool}}\) in the second sentence means “chilly” since it refers to “weather”. So the way we’ll formalize this attention mechanism should allow for different words in the sentence to influence each other.
The “scaled dot-product attention” presented in the paper takes three input matrices:
A query matrix \(\color{purple}Q\)
A key matrix \(\color{darkorange}K\)
A value matrix \(\color{darkgreen}V\)
These matrices have the following dimensions:
\[
\color{purple}Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\text{tokens}}\times{d_k}}\\
\color{darkorange}K\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\text{tokens}}\times{d_k}}\\
\color{darkgreen}V\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\text{tokens}}\times{d_v}}
\]
We’ll define \(d_k\) and \(d_v\) more precisely later, but for now, understand that these represent projections of the original embedding vectors, where \(d_k, d_v < d_{\text{model}}\).
Understanding Q, K, and V Intuitively
To grasp the role of these matrices, think of them as participating in an information exchange system:
Each row of the \(\color{purple}Q\) matrix contains a query vector \(\color{purple}{\mathbf{q}}_i\) for token \(i\). This vector represents what information token \(i\) is “asking for” from other tokens in the sequence.
Each row of the \(\color{darkorange}K\) matrix contains a key vector \(\color{darkorange}{\mathbf{k}}_j\) for token \(j\). This vector represents what information token \(j\) can “offer” to other tokens’ queries.
Each row of the \(\color{darkgreen}V\) matrix contains a value vector \(\color{darkgreen}{\mathbf{v}}_j\) for token \(j\). This vector represents the actual information content that token \(j\) contributes when its key matches a query.
The attention mechanism works by computing how relevant each token \(j\) is to each token \(i\) by measuring the similarity between \(\color{purple}{\mathbf{q}}_i\) and \(\color{darkorange}{\mathbf{k}}_j\). When this similarity is high, token \(i\) will incorporate more of token \(j\)’s value vector \(\color{darkgreen}{\mathbf{v}}_j\) into its contextual representation.
In our example with “cool,” the query vector for “cool” in the first sentence might strongly match key vectors from fashion-related words like “jacket,” causing its representation to shift toward the “fashionable” meaning. Similarly, in the second sentence, “cool” might match strongly with weather-related words, shifting its representation toward the “chilly” meaning.

From Input Embeddings to Attention Matrices
Now that we understand how the scaled dot-product attention mechanism works, a natural question arises: how do we obtain the \(\color{purple}Q\), \(\color{darkorange}K\), and \(\color{darkgreen}V\) matrices in the first place?
In the Transformer architecture, these matrices can be derived in different ways depending on whether we’re computing self-attention or cross-attention. For now, let’s focus on self-attention, as it’s conceptually simpler to grasp. We’ll introduce cross-attention later when discussing the Transformer’s encoder and decoder blocks.
Self-Attention: Same Source, Different Projections
In self-attention, all three matrices \(\color{purple}Q\), \(\color{darkorange}K\), and \(\color{darkgreen}V\) are derived from the same input sequence, which corresponds to the input embeddings, that gets projected through learned linear transformations:
\(\color{purple}{W^{Q}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times{d_k}}\) - Projects input embeddings into query space of dimension \(d_k\).
\(\color{darkorange}{W^{K}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times{d_k}}\) - Projects input embeddings into key space of dimension \(d_k\).
\(\color{darkgreen}{W^{V}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times{d_v}}\) - Projects input embeddings into value space of dimension \(d_v\).
Note that the query and key spaces intentionally share the same dimensionality (\(d_k\)). This is because we compute dot products between queries and keys, which requires matching dimensions. The dimensionality of the values \(d_v\) can be different even though it’s common to have \(d_v=d_k\).
Mathematical Formulation
If we denote our input embeddings as matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{\text{tokens}} \times d_{\text{model}}}\), where \(n_{\text{tokens}}\) is the sequence length and \(d_{\text{model}}\) is the embedding dimension, then:
\[
\color{purple}Q = X\color{purple}{W^Q} \\
\color{darkorange}K = X\color{darkorange}{W^K} \\
\color{darkgreen}V = X\color{darkgreen}{W^V}
\]
With these projections, each token in our sequence now has corresponding query, key, and value vectors. These are then used in the scaled dot-product attention formula we covered earlier.
Multi-Head Attention
The authors of the paper take the scaled dot-product attention concept a step further with Multi-Head Attention, which allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces.
In Multi-Head Attention, instead of performing a single attention function, the model performs attention multiple times in parallel. Each of these parallel attention operations is called a “head”, and each head learns to focus on different aspects of the relationships between tokens.
For each head \(i\) from a total of \(h\) heads, we create separate projection matrices:
\(\color{purple}{W^{Q}_\color{black}i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times{d_k}}\) - Projects input embeddings into query space.
\(\color{darkorange}{W^{K}_\color{black}i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times{d_k}}\) - Projects input embeddings into key space.
\(\color{darkgreen}{W^{V}_\color{black}i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times{d_v}}\) - Projects input embeddings into value space.
Mathematical Formulation
Denoting again our input token embeddings as matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{\text{tokens}} \times d_{\text{model}}}\). For each attention head \(i\), we compute:
\[
\color{purple}Q_i = X\color{purple}{W^Q_{\color{black}i}} \\
\color{darkorange}K_i = X\color{darkorange}{W^K_{\color{black}i}} \\
\color{darkgreen}V_i = X\color{darkgreen}{W^V_{\color{black}i}}
\]
Then, we apply the Scaled Dot Product attention to each head independently:
\[
\text{head}_i = \text{Attention}(\color{purple}Q_i, \color{darkorange}K_i, \color{darkgreen}V_i) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{\color{purple}Q_i\color{darkorange}K_i^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)\color{darkgreen}V_i
\]
The outputs from each head are concatenated and then projected once more using a final output projection matrix \(W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{hd_v \times d_{\text{model}}}\):
\[
\text{MultiHead}(X) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \text{head}_2, \ldots, \text{head}_h)W^O
\]
Why Multiple Heads?
Multiple attention heads allow the model to capture different types of relationships simultaneously:
Some heads might focus on local relationships between adjacent words.
Others might capture long-distance dependencies.
Some might attend to syntactic relationships, while others focus on semantic meaning.
Generally speaking, this approach helps the model build richer representations of the input text.
In practice, the paper uses \(h = 8\) parallel attention heads for the encoder and decoder layers, with \(d_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}}/h = 64\).
Layer Normalization
Layer Normalization is another crucial component of the Transformer architecture that helps stabilize and accelerate training. Unlike Batch Normalization, which normalizes across the batch dimension, LayerNorm operates on the feature dimension for each individual sample.
Mathematical Formulation
For an input vector \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}\) (representing a single token’s embedding), LayerNorm applies the following transformation:
\[
\text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{x}) = \gamma \odot \frac{\mathbf{x} - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} + \beta
\]
Where:
\(\mu = \frac{1}{d_{\text{model}}} \sum_{i=1}^{d_{\text{model}}} x_i\) is the mean of the features
\(\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{d_{\text{model}}} \sum_{i=1}^{d_{\text{model}}} (x_i - \mu)^2\) is the variance of the features
\(\epsilon\) is a small constant added for numerical stability
\(\gamma, \beta \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}\) are learnable parameters (scale and shift)
\(\odot\) denotes element-wise multiplication
When applied to a matrix of token embeddings \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{\text{tokens}} \times d_{\text{model}}}\), LayerNorm processes each row independently, normalizing across the embedding dimension.
The main purpose of Layer Normalization is to prevent exploding or vanishing gradients by ensuring that the input to each sub-layer of the full transformer architecture has consistent statistical properties (that allow for faster convergence as well!).
Feed Forward Layer
The last building block that will help us compose the whole Transformer architecture is the Position-wise Feed Forward Network (FFN). Despite its simplicity, this component contributes significantly to the model’s expressive power.
Mathematical Formulation
The Feed Forward Network consists of two linear transformations with a ReLU activation in between:
\[
\text{FFN}(\mathbf{x}) = \max(0, \mathbf{x}W_1 + b_1)W_2 + b_2
\]
Where:
\(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}\) is the input vector for a single token
\(W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{ff}}}\) and \(W_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ff}} \times d_{\text{model}}}\) are weight matrices
\(b_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ff}}}\) and \(b_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}\) are bias vectors
\(d_{\text{ff}}\) is the inner dimension of the feed-forward network (typically 4 times larger than \(d_{\text{model}}\))
Crucially, this FFN is applied to each position (token) separately and identically - hence “position-wise”. When working with a sequence of tokens represented as a matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{\text{tokens}} \times d_{\text{model}}}\), the FFN processes each row independently, using the same set of parameters \(W_1, b_1, W_2, b_2\).
The Position-wise FFN serves mainly to introduce non-linearity through the ReLU activation, increasing the model’s capacity to learn complex functions.
In the paper, the authors use \(d_{\text{ff}} = 2048\) with \(d_{\text{model}} = 512\), creating a significant expansion in the intermediate representation.
Complete Transformer Architecture
Now that we have a grasp of how the Multi Head Attention, Layer Normalization, and Feed Forward Network blocks work, we can visualize the full Transformer architecture, composed of both an encoder and a decoder block. In the context of neural machine translation, the encoder’s responsibility is to extract information from the original language (e.g., English) sentence, while the decoder has to predict the words (tokens) that will compose the sentence in the target language (e.g., German). We’ll use as an example the following English to German sentence pair:

Encoder Structure
The encoder is composed of a stack of \(N = 6\) identical layers. Each layer has two sub-layers:
A multi-head self-attention mechanism, where \(\color{purple}Q\), \(\color{darkorange}K\), and \(\color{darkgreen}V\) are all derived from the output of the previous layer (or input embeddings for the first layer)
A position-wise fully connected feed-forward network
We employ a residual connection around each of the two sub-layers, followed by layer normalization. That is, the output of each sub-layer is \(\text{LayerNorm}(x + \text{Sublayer}(x))\), where \(\text{Sublayer}(x)\) is the function implemented by the sub-layer itself. To facilitate these residual connections, all sub-layers in the model, as well as the embedding layers, produce outputs of dimension \(d_{\text{model}} = 512\).
Encoder Input during Training
The encoder processes a sequence of tokens with a fixed maximum length, known as the encoder’s context length. This parameter defines the upper limit of input tokens the model can handle in a single forward pass. In our toy example, we set this context length to \(n_e=8\), while the original Transformer paper implementation uses \(n_e=512\) (as seen in the official TensorFlow implementation).
The context length should be chosen to accommodate the longest input sequences expected in your dataset. For sequences shorter than the context length, a special padding token “<PAD>” is added to fill the remaining positions. These padding tokens are typically masked out in the attention mechanism to prevent them from influencing the representations of actual content tokens.
